paragraphs: In South Tyneside, which takes in South Shields, Jarrow, Hebburn, Boldon and Whitburn, children in care are looked after by South Tyneside Council's own fostering service and by independent agencies such as the services shown above.

The council has said plainly that it does not have enough foster carers. In August 2023 it set out plans to recruit and keep more of them, including becoming a foster-friendly employer for its own staff and raising carers' fees and mileage payments to help with the cost of living. It is also one of the twelve councils in Foster with North East, the regional hub backed by the Department for Education. The hub answers first enquiries, and the council's own fostering team then supports you through the application alongside experienced carers from the hub.

South Tyneside is one of a small number of councils running the Mockingbird family model. It links fostering households together in a small local group around a hub, and carers at Levels 2 to 4 of its pay scheme can ask their fostering social worker about joining.

The council pays a weekly allowance for each child to cover their day-to-day costs, and uses a four-level Payment for Skills scheme. Carers at Level 1 receive the allowance only; at Levels 2 to 4 a weekly fee is added for each child, rising with the complexity of the children's needs. Level 4 is for the highest-need and emergency placements and asks that one carer is available full time. Support is available to carers 24 hours a day, there is a one-off grant towards equipment when a child arrives, and a carers' liaison group meets council staff and organises activities. Training runs from the council's own programme to recognised qualifications in care.

Whether you are thinking about the council or an agency, ask each one what it pays at each level, what training it offers and how it supports carers out of hours. Our Tyne and Wear, Gateshead, Sunderland and Newcastle pages cover the neighbouring areas.
